question: Which specific immune cells does HIV attack and destroy?
explanation: Spot on! HIV targets CD4 helper T-cells, which gradually weakens the body's immune defenses. You've got this!

question: Why is HIV prevention so crucial in public health?

options.A: There is currently no absolute cure for the infection
options.B: Medications for the virus are too cheap to manufacture
options.C: Patients refuse to take daily medications once diagnosed
options.D: Prevention completely eliminates all other infectious diseases

explanation: Correct! Since a cure isn't here yet, stopping new infections in the first place is our best tool. Keep up the great thinking!

question: In the classic ABCD HIV prevention strategy, what does the letter 'C' stand for?
explanation: That's right! 'C' stands for consistent condom use, which blocks the exchange of infectious body fluids during sex.

question: A patient asks which part of the ABCD strategy guarantees 100% protection from sexually transmitted HIV. What is the best response?
explanation: Spot on! Complete abstinence is the only strategy that offers absolute protection against sexually transmitted HIV.

question: What does the catchy phrase U=U mean in modern HIV care?
explanation: Brilliant! U=U means when a person's viral load is undetectable through ART, they cannot sexually pass the virus to others.

question: A patient asks how Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) works. How should you explain it?

options.A: It builds a chemical defense in your body so the virus cannot establish an infection if you are exposed
options.B: It permanently boosts your natural red blood cell count to fight off germs
options.C: It numbs nerve endings so you no longer feel any pain during intercourse
options.D: It cures any existing HIV infection within the first week of daily dosing

explanation: You got it! PrEP gives the body a protective chemical shield so the virus can't take hold if exposure happens.

question: Which action is strictly forbidden when handling used injection needles to prevent injuries?

options.B: Placing needles in a puncture-resistant bin
options.D: Carrying a tray with a used syringe

explanation: Correct! Never recap needles by hand—it's a leading cause of accidental needlestick injuries in the clinic.

question: Why do nurses apply universal precautions to every patient, not just those with a known infection?

options.A: Hospital management requires it to save money on lab testing
options.B: Testing blood takes too many days to be useful in an emergency
options.C: Many individuals with infections may be completely unaware or undiagnosed
options.D: Patients get offended if nurses ask about their infection status

explanation: Spot on! Many people carry bloodborne viruses without knowing it, so treating every patient's fluids as potentially infectious keeps everyone safe.

question: What is the maximum window of time to start Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) after a potential HIV exposure?
explanation: That's right! PEP works best when started right away and must be taken within 72 hours to stop the virus from taking hold.

question: A nurse accidentally pricks a finger with a used needle of unknown status. What is the very first thing to do?

options.A: Fill out an incident report form for the hospital human resources
options.B: Begin taking a 28-day course of antibiotics immediately
options.C: Call the patient back to the clinic for a rapid blood test
options.D: Wash the puncture wound thoroughly with soap and clean water

explanation: Correct! Immediate first aid means rushing to wash the site with soap and water to rinse away germs.

question: During which periods can vertical transmission of HIV from mother to child happen?

options.B: During pregnancy, labor, delivery, or breastfeeding
options.C: Only through casual skin-to-skin touch after birth
options.D: Only during the first trimester of pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! The baby can be exposed during pregnancy, birth, or through breast milk afterwards.

question: A pregnant woman tests positive for HIV at her first ANC visit. What is the most important first step to protect her baby?

options.A: Advise her to avoid all forms of physical exercise
options.B: Schedule an immediate cesarean section delivery
options.C: Start her on antiretroviral therapy right away

explanation: You got it! Starting ART early drops her viral load, which is the absolute best way to keep the baby HIV-free.

question: Why is fighting social stigma just as important as medical care in HIV prevention?

options.A: Social attitudes are the only proven cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
options.B: Stigma causes direct physical mutations in the structure of the HIV virus
options.C: Stigma drives people away from getting tested, seeking counseling, and taking medications
options.D: Overcoming stigma eliminates the need for any safe sex practices

explanation: Spot on! When people fear judgment, they hide from testing and treatment, making the spread harder to control.

question: Which of these is a FALSE statement about how HIV spreads that nurses should correct in the community?

options.A: HIV can pass from a mother to her child during breastfeeding
options.B: HIV is easily spread through sharing eating utensils and drinking glasses
options.C: HIV is spread through direct contact with infected blood
options.D: HIV is transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected partner

explanation: Correct! Sharing spoons or cups does not spread HIV because the virus dies quickly outside the body and isn't passed through casual saliva.
